Wall Street just told AI agents: you can look, but you can’t touch.

JPMorgan, Schwab, and Citi all made the same call this month. Outside AI agents can read account data, but they can’t move money. Schwab’s CEO said his firm blocks attempts tens of times a week, and Jamie Dimon warned about rogue agents, possibly thousands of them.

That’s the banking answer to agent risk: read-only, full stop.

Web3 builders are exploring the opposite design: let the agent act, but inside hard limits. Spending caps, allow-lists of approved contracts, permissions that expire on their own. Same fear, different philosophy.

For hiring, that makes one profile unusually valuable: engineers who can design permission systems for software that holds value. Smart contract security, account abstraction, wallet infrastructure, plus a real understanding of how agents fail.

If you’ve built scoped permissions or session-key logic, lead with it.

We’re speaking with teams hiring for exactly this. Reach out if that’s you.

A 37% tech Net Employment Outlook for Q4 means your overseas hire is competing with everyone else's.

Experis Tech Talent Outlook (15 Sep 2026) puts the global tech Net Employment Outlook at 37% for Q4 2026. Employers are prioritising AI capabilities alongside the human skills needed to put them to work.

The common belief: our India brand and brief are enough to win talent abroad. Here is where that breaks down.

1. The pool is shared. Indian companies hiring abroad are bidding for the same people as local employers and everyone else expanding.

2. The ask is two-sided. AI skills plus human skills means a longer screening checklist, and a generalist agency may not know how to test for both.

3. Speed matters more. With demand like this, a slow, scattered process across several agencies and contracts gives candidates time to go elsewhere.

What it means for India TA/HR teams: define the AI skill and the human skill you need for each role before you brief anyone. Send the role to specialists who know that local market. Keep contracts and invoices simple so your team's time goes to candidates.

That is how CBREX works: one contract, 4,000+ specialist recruiting firms across 55 countries, and you pay only when you hire.

Perfect ratings do not answer every hiring question.

An excellent rating can offer useful context without answering the buyer's particular question. They may still need to know whether you have solved a similar problem, understand the constraints and can run the work reliably. Relevance gives general praise a place in the decision. Show the details that connect your history to the current assignment.

A five-star review about a small illustration commission may not explain suitability for a complex product launch. Look for relevant examples and discuss the proposed process. The rating remains useful context, but the new assignment still needs its own evaluation.

1. Select examples close to the client's need.
2. Explain the situation and your contribution.
3. Describe the process the buyer can expect.
4. Use ratings alongside concrete evidence and clear terms.

Build trust around the actual decision being made. A strong overall score should support that evaluation rather than replace it.

The lessons of corporate. 
when organizations face extreme, survival like replacing departments with AI agents—corporate branding like "Great Place to Work" or "Equal Opportunity Employer" often reveals itself to be corporate marketing rather than a safety net.
When a company must cut 30% of its workforce because AI agents can handle the workload, the transition is rarely a pure, objective meritocracy. In high-stakes corporate shifts, the workplace can absolutely feel like a "cowboy zone" where survival depends on internal politics.
Here is a breakdown of why this disconnect happens and how the internal power dynamics actually play out during an AI restructuring:

1. The Myth of the "Clean Slate" External Hire
When a company creates a new, highly coveted AI-native department, outsiders assume the company will post the job publicly and hire the best resume. In reality, leadership almost always defaults to internal allocation first for several survivalist reasons:
$Context over Credentials: Someone who already understands the company's messiest internal data, legacy political factions, and client quirks is highly valuable. They can train the AI agents much faster than a brilliant external prompt engineer who doesn't know where the company's "bodies are buried."
$Risk Mitigation: Hiring externally is a gamble. Moving an internal, trusted political ally into a powerful new AI role protects the executive's own fiefdom.

2. The Illusion of Corporate "Tags" and Certifications
Certifications like Great Place to Work or Equal Opportunity statements are heavily structured compliance frameworks and employer branding tools.
$These awards are largely based on employee sentiment surveys taken during stable times, heavily pushed by HR departments to attract talent. They do not dictate how a board of directors or an executive team will act when a disruptive technology threatens their quarterly profit margins.
$The Reality of "Equal Opportunity": This ensures that the process of hiring and firing follows strict legal guidelines to avoid discrimination lawsuits based on protected classes (race, gender, age, etc.). 
$Fiefdom Building: Managers who control the data pipelines or the budget will position their own loyalists as the "Supervisors" of the new AI tools to ensure their own departments don't lose funding or relevance.
$The "Savior" Narrative: Politically savvy workers position themselves as the bridge between the old world and the new world. They make sure the executives know they are the ones keeping the automated system from crashing.
$Nepotism and Protectionism: When roles contract, executives protect their inner circle. The "middle layer" of average, quiet performers who simply do their jobs without playing the political game are often the most exposed to layoffs

The Takeaway
The corporate messaging paints a picture of an orderly, fair meritocracy, but massive technological disruptions expose the raw, political core of corporate survival.

Anthropic, the AI company behind Claude, published a report examining how artificial intelligence is changing work and employment inside its own organisation.

 💡 Key Takeaways

 1️⃣ Productivity gains - AI is enabling employees to accomplish significantly more work. Engineers are producing 5x more code, sales teams are closing more deals, lawyers process more contracts, admin teams handle higher volumes of work.

 2️⃣ Greater emphasis on human skills - Things like communication, judgement, relationship building and influencing others appear to be becoming more valuable, not less. These are areas where people still have a clear advantage.

 3️⃣ Fewer entry level tech roles - Anthropic has reduced the proportion of junior technical hires, with junior technical hires declining from 27% to 9%. 

 4️⃣ Work was shifting from execution to oversight - Employees increasingly act as managers of AI agents rather than directly performing all tasks themselves. Tasks were growing in other areas such as monitoring AI outputs, writing prompts and reporting.

 5️⃣ Output bottlenecks - AI generates more work than employees can easily review. Anthropic estimates that simply reading all AI generated output could consume over half of an employee's work week. Around 80% of agent session time is spent waiting for human review, decisions, or input.

 6️⃣ Hiring priorities are changing - Hiring managers are putting less emphasis on narrow technical expertise or tradition execution focused skills. Instead, they are increasingly valuing autonomy, judgement, adaptability and high customer and mission orientation

 7️⃣ Employees are automating their own roles away - Employees are increasingly using AI to take over tasks they previously completed themselves, helping to make parts of their own role obsolete. To address this, Anthropic focused on sharing the benefits through broad employee equity ownership, identifying impacted roles early, and prioritising internal mobility and redeployment opportunities. The goal was to ensure employees could benefit from the productivity gains they were helping create.

The productivity gains are hard to ignore, but so are the trade offs. AI is creating more work than humans can realistically review, turning human attention into the new bottleneck. At the same time, some senior roles are shifting from creating and doing the work to reviewing and validating AI outputs.

Questions also remain around the future of entry level opportunities, talent pipelines, job displacement and whether workers will share equally in the productivity gains AI creates, that they often have a role in. Not every employer can offer equity, redeployment programs or significant investment in workforce transition.

2,300 job applications. A Princeton PhD. Still no stable job.

Jack Weis graduated summa cum laude from Rice University and earned a PhD in Chemical Engineering from Princeton University.

His research was cited by the Nobel committee when it announced the 2024 Nobel Prize in Physics.

Yet, since completing his PhD in 2024, he has applied for more than 2,300 jobs without finding stable employment, according to Hindustan Times.

He applied for research positions, explored other industries, contacted university alumni and even worked on training AI systems. That contract eventually ended, too.

His story highlights a reality that many job seekers are experiencing.

A degree from a prestigious university is no guarantee of employment.

Sending hundreds of applications does not guarantee interviews.

Even highly specialised knowledge has limited value if employers are not hiring for it.

And with AI changing the nature of work, the gap between what people learn and what employers need could become more important.

There is also a lesson here for students and fresh graduates.

Don't focus only on collecting degrees and certificates. Build practical skills, understand what employers actually need, and learn to communicate the value you can bring to an organisation.

At the same time, we should not assume that unemployment is always the candidate's fault. Hiring freezes, limited vacancies and changing industry requirements also matter.

Being qualified and being employable are two different things.

The bigger question is this: if someone with these credentials can struggle to find work, what does that mean for the average graduate entering the job market?

Here's a playbook for turning your résumé bullet points into a career story that actually lands.

The bullet point version: "Led product redesign that improved user retention."
The story version: "We were three months from a renewal cliff with our largest account. I ran five user sessions in two weeks, rebuilt the onboarding flow from scratch, and we closed the renewal at 2x the original contract."

Same fact. Completely different signal.

The problem is that most people don't know how to make that translation on their own. Here's the process that works.

Step 1: Pull every role title and company name from your résumé. For each one, answer: what was broken or missing when I arrived? If nothing was broken, why did the role exist?

Step 2: For each project or achievement, answer: what decision did I make that someone else wouldn't have? If you can't name the decision, the story isn't there yet.

Step 3: Add the stakes. Every story needs a number, a deadline, or a named consequence. "Improved retention" is a claim. "Reduced 90-day churn from 34% to 11% before the board review" is evidence.

Step 4: Cut the context no one needs. Hiring managers don't need the company background or the team structure. They need the problem, your call, and what happened.

Step 5: Write one sentence per role that you could say out loud without flinching. If it sounds like a press release, rewrite it. If you'd say it in a conversation, it's done.

This is exactly the kind of story that CraftedBio's AI interview surfaces. It asks targeted follow-up questions for each role — not generic prompts, but questions aimed at pulling out the decision, the stakes, and the outcome you glossed over in the bullet point.

The finished product lives at a clean craftedbio.com/yourname URL. You drop it into an application instead of a PDF and the person on the other side gets the whole story, not the filtered version.

What's the one role on your résumé where the bullet point tells maybe 20% of what actually happened?

🚨 Your RAG application retrieves the correct document.
But should the user be allowed to see it?

That's a question every enterprise .NET + AI team needs to answer.

Imagine building an internal knowledge assistant using ASP.NET Core, Azure OpenAI, and vector search.
An employee asks a question.
The retrieval system finds a highly relevant document.
The LLM generates an accurate answer.
Everything appears to work perfectly.
But there's a problem.
That employee may not have permission to access the original document.
This is why retrieval accuracy alone isn't enough for enterprise RAG.

A production-ready architecture should consider:
✅ Identity-aware document retrieval
✅ Role-Based Access Control (RBAC)
✅ Document-level authorization
✅ Tenant and data isolation
✅ Permission-aware metadata filtering
✅ Secure embedding and vector storage
✅ Prompt injection defenses
✅ Sensitive data masking
✅ Source citations and traceability
✅ Audit logging and access monitoring

One important principle:
Authorization must be enforced before restricted content reaches the LLM context.
Prompt instructions are not a substitute for access controls.

And a highly accurate AI response can still be a security failure if it exposes information the user wasn't entitled to access.

What's the hardest part of implementing enterprise RAG securely?
A) Document-level permissions
B) Retrieval accuracy
C) Data privacy and compliance
D) Monitoring and governance

I was back at SPH Media last week for the recording of OMG, Berita Harian. Had a fun time with Shaza Daliela and her team at the Berita Harian office. I was sharing recent pertinent issues on fresh grad employment in light of the dynamic and chaotic employment landscape impacting them. Let me share my extended views on the matter.

𝗦𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗼 𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗷𝗼𝗯 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻 𝘆𝗼𝘂 𝗹𝗮𝗰𝗸 𝗮𝗯𝗶𝗹𝗶𝘁𝘆 𝗼𝗿 𝗽𝗼𝘁𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗶𝗮𝗹.
That was one message I shared during my recent OMG podcast interview on fresh graduate employment. We explored hiring expectations, AI’s impact on entry-level work, and what graduates and employers can do to bridge the gap.

𝙃𝙚𝙧𝙚 𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙢𝙮 𝙚𝙭𝙩𝙚𝙣𝙙𝙚𝙙 𝙠𝙚𝙮 𝙩𝙖𝙠𝙚𝙖𝙬𝙖𝙮𝙨:
🎖️ Your qualification opens doors. Show what you can contribute.
Go beyond listing certificates. Share examples of initiative, teamwork and problem-solving. Organising an event for 200 students, for instance, can demonstrate project management, coordination and the ability to handle unexpected challenges.
🎖️𝙇𝙚𝙖𝙧𝙣 𝙩𝙤 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠 𝙬𝙞𝙩𝙝 𝘼𝙄
AI is changing tasks and the skills employers value. Learn to use it effectively while strengthening your judgement, communication and ability to make responsible decisions. Employers also have a responsibility to develop young talent as work changes.
🎖️ 𝙀𝙭𝙥𝙚𝙘𝙩𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙢𝙪𝙨𝙩 𝙬𝙤𝙧𝙠 𝙗𝙤𝙩𝙝 𝙬𝙖𝙮𝙨
Graduates should demonstrate curiosity, preparation and willingness to learn. Employers should offer realistic entry-level requirements, guidance and opportunities. Asking fresh graduates for years of experience closes the very door they need to enter.
🎖️𝙔𝙤𝙪𝙧 𝙛𝙞𝙧𝙨𝙩 𝙟𝙤𝙗 𝙘𝙖𝙣 𝙗𝙚 𝙖 𝙨𝙩𝙖𝙧𝙩𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙥𝙤𝙞𝙣𝙩
Consider adjacent roles, contract opportunities, internships or traineeships that offer meaningful learning and reasonable employment terms. Your first role does not determine your entire career.
🎖️𝙄𝙛 𝙖𝙥𝙥𝙡𝙞𝙘𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙤𝙣𝙨 𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙜𝙤𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙣𝙤𝙬𝙝𝙚𝙧𝙚, 𝙧𝙚𝙫𝙞𝙚𝙬 𝙮𝙤𝙪𝙧 𝙖𝙥𝙥𝙧𝙤𝙖𝙘𝙝
No interviews? Revisit your CV and the roles you target. Interviews but no offers? Reflect on how clearly you demonstrate your contribution.

My closing advice: 𝙇𝙀𝘼𝙍𝙉. 𝘼𝘿𝘼𝙋𝙏. 𝙎𝙏𝘼𝙍𝙏.

To fellow employers and hiring managers: 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘄𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗶𝘁 𝘁𝗮𝗸𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝘂𝘀 𝘁𝗼 𝗴𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗺𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗵 𝗴𝗿𝗮𝗱𝘂𝗮𝘁𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗳𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗳𝘂𝗹 𝗼𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁𝘂𝗻𝗶𝘁𝘆?

Italy's AI Act rules get an enforcer on October 23 — and a hard line on automated HR decisions.

Legislative Decree 179/2026, published October 8, completes Italy's implementation of the EU AI Act. The National Cybersecurity Agency (ACN) becomes the market surveillance authority, AgID oversees certification bodies, and fines track the AI Act ceilings — up to €35 million or 7% of worldwide turnover for prohibited practices.

Article 41 matters for every employer in Italy: final decisions on hiring, contract changes, dismissal, discipline, or performance ratings cannot rest solely on automated processing. A person with real, autonomous power must decide — worker consent does not lift the ban, and a dismissal in breach is void.

Takeaway: map which HR decisions your tools influence, and name the human who actually makes — and can change — each final call.

Not wanting to give anyone any nefarious ideas here, but I have a question…

What if the best candidate for a job isn’t actually the most qualified, but simply the best at manipulating AI?

We’re seeing more employers use artificial intelligence to screen résumés, assess qualifications and shortlist candidates.

But here’s something I wonder how many employers have considered.

What if an applicant embeds hidden instructions inside their résumé, specifically designed to convince the AI that they’re an exceptional candidate?

Instructions that a human recruiter might never see, but an AI system could read and potentially follow.

It’s called prompt injection. And it’s not hypothetical.

Researchers presenting at the 2026 USENIX Security Symposium examined approximately 200,000 real-world résumés and found hidden prompt-injection content in about 1% of them.

Separate research has demonstrated that these techniques can influence candidate rankings under certain experimental conditions.

Think about that.

We could potentially be moving from hiring the most qualified candidate to hiring the person who knows how to manipulate the technology evaluating them.

And this raises a much bigger question.

If an AI system can be influenced by instructions hidden in a résumé, what happens when it’s reading contracts, emails, websites, financial documents or patient information?

This is why I keep saying that AI adoption, cybersecurity and AI governance cannot be treated as separate conversations.

It’s not enough to ask what AI can do for your organization.

We also need to ask who or what can influence the decisions it makes.

Because sometimes the biggest risk isn’t what we’ve instructed AI to do.

It’s what someone else has instructed it to do.

There is a procurement pattern in language services that has repeated consistently enough to be predictable.

An organization evaluates vendors. A technology-forward entrant presents a compelling value proposition: AI-driven translation delivering human-quality output at machine speed and significantly reduced cost. The demo performs well on the sample content provided. The pricing model is attractive against the incumbent. The contract gets signed.

The first few months produce acceptable results on high-volume, lower-complexity content. The dashboard metrics are green. The account team is responsive.

Then the complexity arrives. Legal documents where terminology precision carries enforceability weight. Medical communications where register and cultural framing affect patient behavior. Government deliverables where a single mistranslated obligation creates compliance exposure. Educational content where the accuracy gap shows up in community trust metrics before anyone identifies the source.

The AI output is fluent. It is not consistently accurate at the professional standard these contexts require. The gap between those two things is invisible in a demo and visible in production.

The organization begins hiring post-editors. Then senior reviewers. Then subject matter specialist translators. The job listings use language like "quality assurance," "post-editing workflow," and "urgent capacity need." They do not reference the AI platform by name.

Six months after the initial contract, the organization is running a hybrid model that costs more than the incumbent they replaced, produces results that are still being stabilized, and has generated client relationship conversations nobody wanted to have.

This is not a hypothetical. It is a recurring procurement outcome that organizations in every sector experience and rarely discuss publicly because the path back to professional standards is quieter than the announcement that started the cycle.

We use technology thoughtfully. We do not use it as a substitute for the standard.

200+ languages. ISO/ASTM certified. MWBE certified.

The fastest way to double a product team's shipping velocity is not hiring more engineers or writing PRDs with AI.
It is implementing a 60-minute decision rule on two-way doors.
Most enterprise product teams are paralyzed by decision latency. A simple UI change, an experiment threshold, or a lightweight workflow tweak gets dragged through four committee meetings, two architecture syncs, and three weeks of alignment threads.
Why?
Because teams treat reversible decisions with the bureaucracy of irreversible bets.
In Sheet 34 of my book, The Unshakeable Product Manager, I codified a simple framework any product manager can implement tomorrow morning at 9:00 AM:
The Irreversible Decision Rubric
Before you schedule a single alignment meeting or write a 5-page proposal, ask one question:
If this decision fails completely, can we revert it in under 48 hours with zero data corruption and minimal blast radius?
If the answer is YES (a Two-Way Door):
- Cancel the committee meeting.
- The lead product manager or engineer decides in under 60 minutes.
- Ship to a 5% canary cohort or behind a feature flag.
- Learn from live telemetry, not boardroom speculation.
If the answer is NO (a One-Way Door):
This is a database schema migration, a breaking API contract, or an irreversible pricing overhaul.
- Now, and only now, you conduct a formal blast-radius audit.
- You identify failure modes.
- You require named executive sign-off.
What happens when a team implements this single distinction?
1. 40% of recurring meetings vanish overnight.
2. Decision latency drops from weeks to hours.
3. High-ownership engineers stay engaged because they are not trapped in consensus theater.
Velocity is not about typing faster. It is about knowing which decisions deserve a committee and which decisions deserve a timer.
The complete operational rubric and blast-radius checklists are codified in Sheet 34 of The Unshakeable Product Manager.

The hiring process is broken, and most of what's being built is fixing the middle of the problem instead of the root of it.

There are major structural issues – homogeneity in team composition, poor-quality job descriptions, a skills gap within talent organizations, and overreliance on AI tools for efficiency and talent matching; we haven't cracked the code on doing this with a lens for transferable skills vs. keyword search. 

For instance, I started my career in outside sales in the CPG industry, when a human reviewed my resume decades ago at this point, they were able to infer transferability for the role within retail banking. This is not happening today. 

My two cents: we're using school glue and popsicle sticks to hold things together, and adding a new tool, rather than dismantling and rebuilding, starting with who leads & builds the talent organization, who signs off on the enterprise software contract, and ultimately determines what/how resumes actually make it to a human. 

Candidates are auto-applying. Companies are auto-screening. Both sides are automating faster than ever, and neither is touching what job seekers say matters most – respect for their time, transparency, and a fair assessment; 9 in 10 have been ghosted (PeopleScout). 

Only 8% believe AI makes hiring fairer (Greenhouse). And 34% of recruiters spend up to half their week filtering junk applications (Greenhouse), so employers are drowning in a problem the tools helped create.

Fake profiles, AI screening, companies ghosting people. It's the wild, wild west (def said this in my Kool Moe Dee voice).

Here's what I would do: eliminate homogeneity within the talent teams and broader HR organization (you can look up the data on HR organizations), review the incentive structure for TA, have someone outside of the organization audit the tech stack, track false positives & negatives in hiring, hire people who need jobs vs. recycling talent, hire people with fresh perspectives to elevate and challenge legacy thinking.

Ask this final question – why are the people the system screens out the ones companies call when things fall apart?

I’m probably the last person who hasn’t written a LinkedIn post about
 “Will AI take over recruitment from humans?”

AI is already capable of recruiting without a human. Full-cycle.  No question here. 
The technical capability exists.
If the system is properly configured and built, it can, for example, pick up information from an HR system that someone has left and independently start looking for a replacement.

It can publish job ads, source candidates, send messages, arrange meetings, conduct interviews, assess candidates, and send out offers and contracts – all without a human stepping into the workflow, with a new employee hired entirely through AI.

There are legal obstacles – AI cannot actually make hiring decisions on its own, even though it is capable of doing so. Similarly, for example, LinkedIn does not allow certain more extensive activities on its platform, even though AI knows how to carry them out.



Does AI recruit better than a human? Broadly speaking, the answer here is also YES. 
Various studies have now found that AI can recruit better for certain roles where there is more structure and clear validation criteria.

AI can source candidates better and faster than a human, screen CVs more objectively, ask more relevant interview questions, and assess candidates more systematically. 
AI can identify patterns and therefore better assess candidates who would typically be a good fit for a role. 
Where AI struggles today is with anomalies – with assessing potential. 
With someone who, logically speaking, is not a good candidate, but has something about them that outweighs everything else. 
AI is not particularly good at identifying exceptional people and talent. AI is also not the best at building a personal connection.

Broadly speaking, AI is like a very autistic person working in recruitment. 
It cannot sense things, read between the lines, or pick up on what was left unsaid or what is hidden in a silence, a tone of voice, a look, or a handshake. :)

Despite that, AI often wins over humans in recruitment. 


But the biggest obstacle to AI recruitment today is that candidates do not like it.

People themselves prefer an interview with a real person rather than a robot.
Even when the robot is often more polite, more pleasant, and more objective towards the candidate – and doesn’t ghost them.

So the question isn’t whether AI can take over recruitment. Yes, it can.
The question is: should it?

I was reading Anthropic's new report on how work is changing inside their own company, and a few charts in the paper made me pause.

Their total workforce tripled over the last year. Yet the share of technical hires going to junior roles dropped from 27% in early 2025 down to 9%.

A few other numbers from their internal charts stood out to me:

● In February, humans still logged far more working hours than AI agents.
● By August, the company averaged 6 hours of agent activity for every 1 human hour (and 19 hours to 1 inside their research teams).
● Over six months, code commits per engineer grew fivefold and legal contracts processed per person tripled.
● Claude now spends 80% of interactive sessions waiting for a person to check its work.

Because AI handles so much of the daily execution, their hiring managers now focus much more on autonomy and good judgment.

And this is where I get stuck. I am fascinated by how fast this is moving, and at the same time baffled by one major paradox:

How does anyone gain the experience needed to become a senior supervisor if the bottom rungs of the career ladder no longer exist?

When I look back at my own early career, I certainly did not have senior judgment on day one. I only learned how to spot a bad assumption because I spent years doing slow beginner tasks, making mistakes, and fixing them.

Anthropic's employees expect AI to do 75% of their work by 2030.

Maybe I am missing something obvious, but if we remove the junior layer now, I struggle to see where our future experts will come from. If we skip the apprentice stage, how will the next generation learn enough to know when the machine is wrong?

(Links to the blog post and the paper with the charts in the comments.)

🛡️ Now Hiring: Prompt Engineer / LLM Engineer - Python & Text-to-Query
📍 LATAM (Fully Remote) | Long-Term Contract

If you have strong Python development skills and proven expertise in production-level prompt engineering, this is a unique opportunity to evolve a natural-language query prototype into a robust enterprise feature. Our client is seeking a hands-on Prompt / LLM Engineer to build a safe, explainable, and measurable Text-to-Query solution.

Core Responsibilities & Requirements:
✅ Prompt Engineering: Design, maintain, and version sophisticated prompts encompassing domain taxonomies, query grammar, examples, and robust guardrails.
✅ Text-to-Query Systems: Develop natural-language-to-query solutions (e.g., Text-to-SQL, Solr, Elasticsearch) utilizing structured LLM outputs, few-shot prompting, and domain vocabulary handling.
✅ Python Development: Leverage 2+ years of Python experience to build components for prompt assembly, structured intent parsing, query generation, and output validation.
✅ Evaluation & Testing: Build and maintain comprehensive evaluation harnesses to measure accuracy, latency, and cost, establishing rigorous regression testing for model and system changes.
✅ Architecture & Security: Evaluate multi-provider LLM APIs and design secure architectures ensuring generated queries execute safely without exposing protected or row-level data.
✅ Production Experience: Demonstrate hands-on experience deploying LLM solutions in a shipped or production product, moving beyond experimental or proof-of-concept phases.

(Preferred: Apache Solr query construction expertise, healthcare/EMS terminology such as NEMSIS/ICD, fine-tuning small models, and exposure to Azure AI/Microsoft Fabric).

📩 To apply: Please submit your resume detailing your Python development and production LLM expertise to info@connecttechtalent.com

📱 Stay updated on our latest opportunities! Join our WhatsApp channel here: https://lnkd.in/gTYfwJdu
.
